zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. [Dataset](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html); [license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The scan remains authoritative for letters, typeface, marks, spacing and line division.

lines.note: Continues the preceding rope entry with gathering or taking up the rope. The next example begins Nauaga qi-, whose divided verb is completed on the following physical row.
Nauaga qiruru means that the rope breaks. The second example begins Nauauo, the rope as the object of the verb below; neither fragment is a separate headword.

runs.text: Fazer cordas torcendo entre as palmas

lines.note: Nauauo nǒ means making rope by twisting; the Portuguese specifies working between the palms. Preserve the printed caron on ǒ rather than substituting a modern form of the verb.
Das mãos completes entre as palmas: the cord is twisted between the palms of the hands. This short continuation is a complete physical row.
Naua ami is a net made from ropes, as the Portuguese directly states. The visible separation between Naua and ami is retained.

runs.text: O que tẽ a corda na mão do que eſ-

lines.note: Nauadori denotes the person holding the rope attached to someone who is bound. The definition continues after the divided eſ-; tẽ retains its abbreviation tilde.
Tà amarrado completes eſtà amarrado, identifying the bound person whose rope the nauadori holds. The grave accent belongs to the printed continuation.
Nauaguire is a piece or length of rope. The Japanese compound and the Portuguese pedaço de corda support the reading without supplying a more specific length.
Nauaſaqi is the end of a rope; the tall medial letter is long ſ, not f. Ponta da corda supplies the direct gloss.
Nauate is a path between the cultivated low-lying fields. Dantre and varzeas are retained as printed rather than modernized.
Nauatemichi repeats the preceding path-between-fields meaning through Idem. The extra michi element does not require an additional Portuguese definition.

runs.text: Varzea, ou lugar onde ſe ſemea a

lines.note: Nauaxiro names a rice nursery or seedbed. The definition starts with a plot where rice is first sown and continues with the later transplanting operation.

runs.text: primeira vez o arroz pera depois em erua ſe

lines.note: Rice is first sown here so that it can subsequently be transplanted while still green. The dotted i and the surrounding letters support depois, correcting OCR depots.
Deſpor completes the nursery-bed definition: setting out or transplanting the young rice. It is not an omitted new entry despite occupying a short row.
Nauo is the adverb meaning more or further. Adu. belongs to the italic grammatical apparatus, not the Japanese headword.
Nauomotte is another adverb with the same meaning as Nauo. Idem explicitly refers back to the preceding entry.
Nauonauo intensifies the preceding adverb: more and more. The repeated Japanese element corresponds to the repeated Portuguese mais.

Nauori here means recovering from illness, illustrated by Yamaiga nauotta on the following row. Reinspection against the nearby nauotta and otta types shows a badly abraded first t between o and the clear second t; otta is adopted instead of the OCR ota. This restoration remains a damaged-glyph caveat, not an inferred modernization. The printed grave in Sàrar is preserved.

runs.text: Eſtà ja bẽ, ou são da infirmidade.

lines.note: Yamaiga nauotta states that the illness has healed, rendered as being well or free from the illness. The example does print doubled tt, in contrast to the preceding abbreviated ota.
The second Nauori entry concerns correction or restoration rather than healing. It prints otta and introduces additional applications after Item.
The correction can be physical: straightening a leaning house. The scan reads inclinada, restoring the l omitted in the OCR's incinada.
Cajega nauoru describes the wind changing. The printed j is retained; the Portuguese vento establishes the referent without normalizing the Japanese spelling.
Zani nauoru means moving into one's proper place or seat. Porſe is printed as one word, and the Portuguese phrase continues with the place in the room below.
The room is called Zaxiqui within the Portuguese explanation. Fonreǒni nauoru then begins a new example concerning restoration to one's original lands or income.

runs.text: Ser reſtituido a ſuas terras, ou renda.

lines.note: Completes Fonreǒni nauoru: being restored to one's lands or revenue. The gloss concerns restitution, not merely recovery from disease.
The noun Nauoxi is equated with Fitatare and described as a kind of garment. It is distinct from the correcting verb that follows; preserve the printed compact Certalaya and the unexpanded q̃.
The garment is worn over other clothing. Por cima completes the preceding description rather than naming a further garment.
The verb Nauoxi means correcting or putting right. Aya- begins Ayamari, the fault or error corrected in the example; the principal part oita is retained as historical morphology.
Ayamariuo nauoſu means correcting a fault. The next sense begins with abbreviated Itẽ; its tilde is retained without expansion.

runs.text: Mudar a couſa a outro lugar. ¶

lines.note: An additional sense is moving something to another place. Nacauo starts a separate example about restoring friendly relations, continued below.
Nacauo nauoſu is making peace or restoring friendship. Rǒnin begins the next example, concerning the return of an exile or displaced person.
Rǒnin uo nauoſu is glossed as restoring or bringing back the exile. The scan supports reduzir, not OCR redugir; deſter- continues into rado below.
Rado completes deſterrado. Iyeuo nauoſu starts the house-straightening example, with Portuguese ca- divided across the next physical boundary.

runs.text: ſa que eſtaua torta, ou inclinada.

lines.note: Completes caſa: the house had been crooked or leaning. This is the transitive counterpart of the leaning-house sense under Nauori.
Nauozari and nauozarini are glossed as for the most part or approximately. The alternative marker l is Latin editorial apparatus, not a Japanese syllable.
Ou pouco mais, ou menos completes the approximate or general sense. It explains the preceding adverbial alternatives rather than beginning a new entry.
Nauozarina and nauozarino describe something ordinary or middling. The Portuguese medi- continues into mediocre on the next row.

runs.text: ocre, ou de pouco mais, ou menos.

lines.note: Ocre completes mediocre; the rest gives the approximate, neither particularly good nor bad sense. Preserve the physical division instead of joining the Portuguese word in the transcription.
Nauozari narazarugui describes something not ordinary. The negative narazaru is consistent with Portuguese não; the final gui is retained as printed.
Completes the contrast: not an ordinary thing, but a very great one. The line belongs to the preceding negative expression, not the following adverbial entry.
Nauozari narazu is glossed as greatly or beyond the ordinary. It is a separate expression from the preceding attributive narazaru construction.
Ordinario completes fora do ordinario. This short line is retained as running text rather than folded into the next pear entry.
Naxi here names pears. The following identical-looking headword is a verb, so the separate entry and full stop matter.
The verb Naxi means doing or making. Atauo naſu is the first example, explained below as doing harm; aita is the printed historical principal part.
Fazer mal translates Atauo naſu. The next example joins the matrimonial bond, Fufuno chiguiri, with the alternative catarai split after ca-.
Taraiuo completes cataraiuo, and naſu governs the preceding matrimonial expressions. The Portuguese gloss explicitly concerns matrimonial intercourse.

Guegiuo naſu concerns giving orders as a master to a servant, with the servant on the next column's first row. The worn initial retains the inner feature of G, supporting Guegiuo rather than OCR Cuegiuo.
A criado completes the master-to-servant command from the previous column. Reiuo naſu begins making a reverence; re- is the start of its divided Portuguese gloss.
Uerencia completes reuerencia. Samatagueuo naſu means causing an obstruction, with Empe- continued as empedir on the next row.
Dir completes empedir, followed by the equivalent fazer eſtoruo. Tacumiuo naſu starts the next example, which the following line glosses as inventing.
Inuentar translates Tacumiuo naſu. Icariuo naſu is then glossed Agaſtarſe, becoming angry; the initial I and historical spelling are preserved.
This separate Naxi entry means paying rather than simply doing. Voimonouo names the debt paid in the example completed below.
Voimonouo naſu means paying the debt. The printed adiuida remains compact; no modernized spelling or editorial word boundary is imposed.
Naxicudaſare is an honorific giving or issuing verb, used of a noble person. The principal forms and the Portuguese social qualification are retained.
Xenjiuo naxi cudaſareta concerns a superior issuing an order or decree. Feiq. is the upright citation label; the Portuguese translation begins with the divided Mã-.
Dou completes Mãdou: his highness or lordship commanded. The honorific subject explains the elevated verb in the Japanese example.
Naxigi is gold sprinkled over lacquer, named Vruxi inside the Portuguese explanation. Naxi- begins the repeated term in the next example.
Naxigiuo maqu describes applying the speckled gold finish. Dourar deſta maneira refers to the technique just defined, not a generic unrelated gilding operation.
Naximono is a prepared food made from entrails and other small fish parts. The definition continues below with the salting qualification.
The small parts of the fish are salted. This completes the food definition without identifying a particular species or modern recipe.
Naxino qi is the pear tree, distinguished from Naxi, the fruit, in the preceding column. Pereira is the direct Portuguese equivalent.
Naxivchi yeboxi names a kind of cap. The Portuguese compares its shape and material on the following rows rather than giving a modern costume classification.

runs.text: como caraminholas de papel vruxado que v-

lines.note: The caps resemble caraminholas and are made of lacquered paper. The scan reads vruxado, with r after v, not OCR vxuxado; the final v- begins vſão below.
São completes vſão: these caps are used in plays or performances. The reference is to use in autos, not to a separate object named São.
This Naxxo is explained by Voſamuru tocoro and introduces a monastic office. Voſamuru is worn but the surviving letters and the following steward gloss support the supplied reading.

runs.text: ſeruir entre os Bonzos como deſpenſeiro, &c.

lines.note: The office serves the Buddhist clergy in the manner of a steward or storekeeper. Bonzos belongs to the Portuguese description, not to an added Japanese headword.

runs.text: O pagarem os lauradores o rendimẽ-

lines.note: The second Naxxo concerns cultivators paying the revenue from their land. The abbreviated rendimẽ- continues into the next row.

runs.text: to das terras ao ſenhor. Vt,

lines.note: The revenue is paid to the lord. Nenguuo nax- begins the example of paying the annual due, completed by xoſuru below.
Xoſuru completes naxxoſuru; Idem returns to the land-payment definition. This is a continuation of the example, not another headword.
Nayamaxi is glossed as maltreating or persecuting. The supplied principal-form letter u is visibly printed and is not silently expanded to an expected ſu.
Guir completes perſeguir. Cocorouo nayamaſu means afflicting the heart or mind; the Portuguese object follows on the next physical row.
O coração completes afflicting the heart. Tamiuo nayamaſu begins oppressing the common people; its Portuguese verb is divided after Opri-.
Mir completes oprimir, and the objects are the cultivators or people. This confirms the social oppression sense of the Japanese example.
Nayami means being weakened or afflicted. Enlargement shows ǒda, with a d ascender, rather than OCR ǒta; preserve the printed contracted historical principal part.
The person is worn out as though ill. This continuation completes the debilitated-state definition and is distinct from the ceremonial term below.
Nayarai, alternatively Voniyarai, introduces the ceremony for driving away demons. The description continues across five rows; l remains the printed alternative marker.

runs.text: os gentios no principio do anno botando graõs

lines.note: The ceremony occurs at the beginning of the year and includes scattering grain. The enlarged final word reads graõs, with the tilde over o, unlike grãos two rows below.

runs.text: torrados pera o àr dentro de caſa, & depois

lines.note: The grains are roasted and thrown into the air inside the house. The printed grave in àr is preserved rather than changed to modern unaccented ar.

runs.text: comendo cada hum da quelles grãos tantos,

lines.note: Afterwards each participant eats some of those grains. Da quelles retains the printed separation, and grãos here carries its tilde on a.

runs.text: quantos annos cada hum tem, & iſto pera que

lines.note: The number eaten matches each person's years of age. The final clause introduces the protective purpose explained on the next line.
The stated purpose is to prevent the demon from approaching the house. This reports the dictionary's account of the ceremony, not an endorsement of its effect.

runs.text: Arroz em erua pouco crecido q̃ ſe despoẽ.

lines.note: Naye denotes young rice seedlings that are transplanted. The scan prints round s in despoẽ, in contrast to the following line's long ſ; both forms are preserved separately.

runs.text: ¶ Itẽ, ortaliça q̃ ſe deſpoẽ, como cebolinho.

lines.note: The term also covers transplanted vegetable seedlings, with young onions as the example. Itẽ and q̃ remain unexpanded abbreviations.
A separate Naye denotes an earthquake. Nayega yuru is the corresponding example, not the seedling noun from the preceding entries.
Tremer a terra translates Nayega yuru: the earth trembles. The short translation occupies its own physical row.
The verb Naye concerns bodily paralysis or loss of function. The initial Portuguese word has a long ſ in Eſtar; the Japanese uru and eta principal forms are retained.

runs.text: ou aleijado, & ſem ſentir algum membro.

lines.note: The definition includes being disabled and having no sensation in a limb. This continues the bodily sense rather than the later figurative comparison.
Axi, tega nayuru applies the condition to feet and hands. The Portuguese noun for paralysis is divided after parle-.

runs.text: ſia, ou aleijão nos pees, ou nas mãos. ¶ I-

lines.note: ſia completes parleſia; the feet and hands are explicitly named. I- begins Item introducing the figurative extension below.

runs.text: tem, per met. Eſtar como morto, ou ſem

lines.note: The figurative sense is being as though dead or motionless. Per met. belongs to the italic explanatory apparatus and is not expanded in the transcription.

Bulir means moving, completing the motionless-state explanation; the initial b corrects OCR h. The quotation begins Deini nayetaru vuono go-, comparing the captives to enfeebled fish in mud; the fish word begins with printed v, not OCR u.
Tocunite completes gotocunite, the comparison, followed by being captured alive. Sanbiacu yo- begins the number of more than three hundred people.
Nin completes the human numeral phrase. Taif. is the citation label and Lib. 18 gives the book number; the translation begins Mais de trezen-.

runs.text: tos, que forão tomados viuos eſtauão como pei

lines.note: Tos completes trezentos: more than three hundred taken alive were like fish. The scan supports eſtauão, restoring the omitted u in OCR eſtaão. Pei continues as xes at the next page opening; the lower repeated xes is the catchword, not an extra body row.
